item.title: alibaba/open-code-review
item.description:
Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

https://open-codereview.ai

OpenCodeReview

English | 简体中文 | 日本語 | 한국어 | Русский | Türkçe | Français | Tiếng Việt

What is Open Code Review?

Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool. It originated as Alibaba Group's internal official AI code review assistant — over the past two years, it has served tens of thousands of developers and identified millions of code defects. After thorough validation at massive scale, we incubated it into an open source project for the community. Simply configure a model endpoint to get started.

It reads Git diffs, sends changed files to a configurable LLM via an agent with tool-use capabilities, and generates structured review comments with line-level precision. The agent can read full file contents, search the codebase, inspect other changed files for context, and produce deep reviews — not just surface-level diff feedback. Beyond diff review, ocr scan reviews entire files for auditing unfamiliar codebases or directories that have no meaningful diff.

Visit the official website for more details.

Benchmark

Compared to general-purpose agents (Claude Code), Open Code Review achieves significantly higher Precision and F1 with the same underlying model, while consuming only ~1/9 of the tokens and completing reviews faster. Note that its Recall is lower than general-purpose agents — a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise.

A real-world code review benchmark built from 50 popular open-source repositories, 200 real Pull Requests, and 10 programming languages — cross-validated by 80+ senior engineers (1,505 annotated ground-truth issues).

Explore the AACR-Bench dataset on Hugging Face.

Metric What it measures Why it matters
F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall Best single number for overall review quality
Precision Proportion of reported issues that are real defects Higher = fewer false alarms to triage
Recall Proportion of real defects that are found Higher = fewer issues slip through review
Avg Time Wall-clock time per review Matters for CI pipeline latency
Avg Token Total tokens consumed per review Directly impacts API cost

Why Open Code Review?

The Problem with General-Purpose Agents

If you've used general-purpose agents like Claude Code with Skills for code review, you've likely encountered these pain points:

  • Incomplete coverage — On larger changesets, agents tend to "cut corners," selectively reviewing only some files and missing others.
  • Position drift — Reported issues frequently don't match the actual code location, with line numbers or file references drifting off target.
  • Unstable quality — Natural-language-driven Skills are hard to debug, and review quality fluctuates significantly with minor prompt variations.

The root cause: a purely language-driven architecture lacks hard constraints on the review process.

Core Design: Deterministic Engineering × Agent Hybrid

Open Code Review's core philosophy is to combine deterministic engineering with an agent, each handling what it does best.

Deterministic Engineering — Hard Constraints

For review steps that must not go wrong, engineering logic — not the language model — guarantees correctness:

  • Precise file selection — Determines exactly which files need review and which should be filtered, ensuring no important change is missed.
  • Smart file bundling — Groups related files into a single review unit (e.g., message_en.properties and message_zh.properties are bundled together). Each bundle runs as a sub-agent with isolated context — a divide-and-conquer strategy that stays stable on very large changesets and naturally supports concurrent review.
  • Fine-grained rule matching — Matches review rules to each file's characteristics, keeping the model's attention sharply focused and eliminating information noise at the source. Compared to purely language-driven rule guidance, template-engine-based rule matching is more stable and predictable.
  • External positioning and reflection modules — Independent comment-positioning and comment-reflection modules systematically improve both the location accuracy and content accuracy of AI feedback.

Agent — Dynamic Decision-Making

The agent's strengths are concentrated where they matter most — dynamic decisions and dynamic context retrieval:

  • Scenario-tuned prompts — Prompt templates deeply optimized for code review, improving effectiveness while reducing token consumption.
  • Scenario-tuned toolset — Distilled from deep analysis of tool-call traces in large-scale production data — including call frequency distributions, per-tool repetition rates, and the impact of new tools on the overall call chain — resulting in a purpose-built toolset that is more stable and predictable for code review than a generic agent toolkit.

How to Use

Prerequisites

  • Operating system: Windows, macOS, or Linux.
  • Git >= 2.41 — Open Code Review relies on Git for diff generation, code search, and repository operations.

Agent Skills

Use the skills in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Kimi Code, or another agent that supports Agent Skills and can run local commands. Both modes require Git >= 2.41 and the ocr CLI; only native mode requires an OCR model provider.

1. Install the Skills

Run in the project you want to review, then select the skills you need and your agent in the installer:

npx skills add alibaba/open-code-review

The skills guide your agent to install ocr if it is missing, subject to your environment's permissions. You can also install it ahead of time with npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review. Prefer a plugin or manual installation? See the agent-specific setup guide, or copy the desired folders from skills/ into your agent's skill directory.

2. Choose a Review Mode

Native mode Delegation mode
Skill open-code-review open-code-review-delegate
Who reviews? OCR's specialized review agent and pipeline Your current coding agent, following OCR's review pipeline and guardrails
Model and authentication OCR's own provider configuration Your host agent's existing model and authentication
Choose it when You have a model endpoint for OCR and want its full review pipeline You have no separate API key, or want to use your existing agent subscription/setup

No separate key? Start with delegation mode. It skips OCR provider setup, not the host agent's own authentication, usage limits, or costs. A host-agent subscription is not automatically an API credential for native mode. In delegation mode, OCR's CLI and skill together provide the review pipeline and guardrails: file selection, rule resolution, coverage requirements, and structured reporting. The host agent performs analysis, positioning, and reporting within that workflow; it does not run OCR's full native pipeline.

For native mode, configure a provider once with ocr config provider and ocr config model. Authentication depends on the provider; see Configuration.

CLI

Install

npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review

After installation, the ocr command is available globally.

For other installation methods (install script, GitHub Release binary, from source), see Installation.

Quick Start

1. Configure LLM

You must configure an LLM before reviewing code, unless you use Delegation Mode.

  • OCR calls the model: ocr review, the /open-code-review:review command, and the open-code-review skill use OCR's own provider configuration, not your Claude Code Team/Pro subscription login. Authentication requirements depend on the provider; see Configuration.
  • The host agent calls the model: the /open-code-review:delegate-review command and the open-code-review-delegate skill use the host agent's configured model and authentication. No separate LLM configuration or credentials are needed in OCR. See the Claude Code install steps.
ocr config provider          # Select a built-in provider or add a custom one
ocr config model             # Pick a model for the active provider

The interactive UI guides you through provider selection, API key entry, and model configuration, then automatically tests connectivity.

For CLI setup, environment variables, custom providers, and other advanced configuration, see Configuration.

2. Review

cd your-project

# Workspace mode — review all staged, unstaged, and untracked changes
ocr review

# Current branch — review changes since it diverged from main (--to defaults to HEAD)
ocr review --from main

# Branch range — reviews feature-branch's changes since it diverged from main (merge-base mode)
ocr review --from main --to feature-branch

# Single commit
ocr review --commit abc123

# Resume an interrupted range or commit review
ocr session list
ocr review --from main --to feature-branch --resume <session-id>

# Full-file scan — review whole files instead of a diff (no git history needed)
ocr scan                          # scan the entire repository
ocr scan --path internal/agent    # scan a directory or specific files
ocr scan --resume <session-id>   # resume an interrupted full-file scan

# Save results to a file (recommended for AI host agents)
ocr review --format json --output result.json

# Delegation mode — let your AI coding agent perform the review itself
# OCR handles file selection and rule resolution; no LLM configuration needed
ocr delegate preview
ocr delegate rule src/main.go src/handler.go

Documentation

Full documentation lives at open-codereview.ai/docs:

  • Quickstart — install and run your first review
  • Installation — all platforms and package managers
  • CLI Reference — every command and flag
  • Review Rules — customize review rules with path filtering and targeting
  • Configuration — config keys and environment variables
  • MCP Server — extend the review agent with external tools
  • Coding Agent Integrations — choose the platform you use
    • Claude Code — install a plugin with review slash commands
    • Codex — install a plugin with callable review skills
    • Cursor — install a plugin with portable review skills
    • Kimi Code — install a plugin with review slash commands and skills
    • OpenCode — install native review tools and slash commands
    • QCA Forward — run delegation mode with the QCA host model and a ready-to-publish template
    • Skill-compatible agents — install the portable agent skill
  • Review Execution Modes — after integration, choose which LLM performs the review
    • Default (OCR-managed) — OCR runs the review using its configured LLM
    • Delegation Mode — your coding agent runs the review using its own LLM; no OCR API key required
  • CI/CD Integration — GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, GitFlic CI, and Gerrit integration
  • Session Viewer — browse and replay review sessions in browser, mark comments as fixed or ignored and hide them while you work through the findings
  • Telemetry — OpenTelemetry integration for observability
  • FAQ — common questions and troubleshooting

Contributing

This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup, coding guidelines, and how to submit pull requests.

item.title: agent-substrate/substrate
item.description:
Agent Substrate: the core system

https://ate.dev/

Agent Substrate

Zero-trust sandboxing for millions of agents on Kubernetes.

Quickstart · Security · Architecture · Contributing

What is Agent Substrate?

Agent Substrate is a security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. Purpose-built for the era of autonomous agents, Substrate delivers fast resume operations in less than 500ms, with more than 500 activations per second. Agents get isolated compute, identity, networking, and storage. Sensitive credentials are kept out of reach from untrusted code. It supports multiple sandbox technologies, including microVMs and gVisor, while enabling a consistent lifecycle and management of all sandboxes.

At its core, Agent Substrate maps a larger set of “actors” (stateful workloads such as agents) onto a smaller pool of ready “workers”. Because agents spend most of their lives waiting on models, tools, or humans, Substrate snapshots idle actors out of memory and restores them when a request arrives.

Substrate is a low-opinion runtime, not an agent SDK. The workloads it runs do not have to be AI agents, though autonomous, untrusted, mostly-idle agents are the target for its isolation and scheduling model. It runs on standard Kubernetes: Pods, autoscaling, NetworkPolicies. It adds agent-specific scheduling, snapshotting, identity, and network mediation. This allows agentic, inference, training, and reinforcement learning workloads to share one infrastructure plane.

Security Model

Substrate treats every actor as untrusted and mutually hostile, so tenants can share physical nodes without sharing a security boundary. Every control operates within the cold-start and resume budget. See the Security Guide for the full list of security principles and threat model.

  • Always sandboxed, VM-grade boundaries: Every actor runs inside a dedicated gVisor (runsc) or Cloud Hypervisor microVM sandbox with segregated compute, network, and storage. Plain Linux containers are not supported.
  • Per-agent cryptographic identity: Every active actor receives a short-lived SPIFFE X.509 certificate by default, and the egress gateway can mint per-actor JWTs on demand when an egress policy calls for one. Both carry the actor identity and atespace (the Substrate namespace grouping), and are designed to federate with external identity systems.
  • Zero credentials in the sandbox: Actors never hold actor identity JWTs/certs, API keys, or cloud tokens. The built-in egress gateway (atenet-egress) injects credentials into approved outbound requests outside the sandbox, so a prompt-injected or compromised agent has nothing to exfiltrate.
  • Default-deny networking: Actors start with a private network stack, no inbound path except through the ingress router (atenet-router), no lateral actor-to-actor or control-plane access, and outbound traffic restricted by the egress gateway.
  • Pluggable policy at the edge: The egress gateway acts as an external Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that is fully replaceable, allowing you to attach your own authorization, DLP, prompt-injection scanning, or cloud IAM policy engine without placing policy code inside the untrusted sandbox.

Performance & Multiplexing

Watch the Agent Substrate cluster multiplex ~250 stateful actors across just 8 physical pods.

This demo highlights the core developer experience and "Agentic Infrastructure" capabilities of Substrate:

  1. Actor Teleport: Suspend and resume actors onto any available worker in the pool, when needed.
  2. Full-State Persistence: Working memory (RAM) and filesystem state are captured in snapshots and restored intact across hibernation cycles, without losing in-flight sessions or tool state.
  3. 10x–30x Oversubscription: Multiplex a large registry of stateful actors onto a small pool of warm worker pods, paying for compute only while an agent is actively thinking or executing a tool.

To reproduce this demo in your own cluster, see the Counter Demo. For more walkthroughs, visit the agent-substrate YouTube channel.

Star History

Framework Agnostic & Compatibility

Agent Substrate is framework and agent harness agnostic. Because it runs standard OCI container images inside gVisor or microVM sandboxes and enforces security outside the workload, it hosts agents built on any stack without SDK changes:

  • Agent Development Kit (ADK): Preserves session state across invocations as actor state.
  • LangChain: Drop-in execution environment for LangChain agents and tool calls.
  • Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity: High-density, stateful coding environments that keep system and filesystem state across sessions while isolating untrusted code execution.
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP): Deploy sandboxed MCP servers as Substrate Actors with per-actor identity and egress controls.

Ecosystem & Examples

  • Agent Executor: A distributed agent runtime that demonstrates building a secure, hyper-scalable agent harness on Agent Substrate (see the announcement blog and integration guide).
  • kagent: A CNCF Sandbox project and Kubernetes-native framework for building, deploying, and managing AI agents that uses Agent Substrate to run sandboxed, stateful agent workloads (see the announcement blog).

Status and compatibility

Agent Substrate has reached 1.0. We are committed to compatibility and stability of the public API, CLI, and configuration formats. We will continue to add new features, but we will not break existing APIs or configuration formats without a major version bump. See "Compatibility and schema evolution" in CONTRIBUTING.md for more details.

Supported Kubernetes Releases

Currently we aim to support the latest stable release of Kubernetes, and the previous minor release.

Community

For announcements, technical discussions, and community support, please join the ate-dev Google Group.

We host a weekly community meeting every Thursday from 10:00am - 11:00am PST.

  • Video call link: https://meet.google.com/uhq-cxvn-dhy
  • Or dial: (US) +1 253-289-6971 PIN: 787 664 574 59#
  • More phone numbers: https://tel.meet/uhq-cxvn-dhy?pin=9044088223662
  • Meeting notes for the weekly sync meeting
  • Recordings and transcripts of all community meetings

We also have channels in the CNCF slack; request an invite here if you don't have access.

  • #substrate-users to discuss using substrate.
  • #substrate-dev to discuss developing substrate.

Developing

Please see CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines on contributing to the project. We welcome contributions of all kinds, but the project is VERY young. Our immediate focus is on building out the core system and demos, so we may not be able to review or merge contributions that don't align with those goals in the near term.

Quickstart (Development)

To quickly set up the complete environment:

  1. Make sure you have Go, kubectl, and docker installed and configured on your dev machine. We will automatically manage other dependencies via Go, including kind. A Linux host that will run more than about a thousand sandboxes also needs a larger kernel neighbor table (net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1/2/3 = 4096/16384/32768); hack/create-kind-cluster.sh warns when the host is at the default of 1024.

  2. Run the following steps:

# create cluster and local registry
hack/create-kind-cluster.sh

# make ate-setup target the kind cluster; set this in every shell that runs
# ate-setup, including for the demo walkthroughs
export ATE_INSTALL_KIND=true

# install Substrate
go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy ate-system --credential-provider='{"name":"k8s.io"}' \
  --ingress-allowed-spiffe-ids=spiffe://cluster.local/ns/ate-system/sa/atenet-client

# install counter demo
go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy demo counter

# install kubectl-ate
go install ./cmd/kubectl-ate

# create a counter actor in the demo's atespace (--template names the
# actor template, resolved in the actor's atespace)
kubectl ate create actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter --template counter

# serve a local proxy on port 8000 that sends requests to the actor through the
# network router
kubectl ate proxy actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter

Important

{"name":"k8s.io"} deploys the bundled credential provider with an empty, default-deny namespace policy. Before an actor can have a credential injected, grant its atespace the namespaces whose Secrets it may read; see Enable it.

  1. In a separate terminal, send an HTTP request to increment the counter:
curl -X POST -i http://localhost:8000/

Custom Setup and Deployment

You can deploy or cleanup specific Agent Substrate components using the installation script. See go run ./cmd/ate-setup for all options.

# Re-deploy only ate-apiserver of the ATE system
go run ./cmd/ate-setup deploy apiserver

# Delete everything (core system and all demos)
go run ./cmd/ate-setup delete all

Tearing down local kind resources

If you need to delete the local kind cluster and its registry (if it was created by hack/create-kind-cluster.sh):

./hack/delete-kind-cluster.sh

GKE Quickstart

To deploy on Google Kubernetes Engine, follow the official GKE Installation Guide. It lists the prerequisites and gives the one-line installer command. The installer's source and detailed options are in substrate-gke.

Demos

We provide several sample applications demonstrating Agent Substrate's capabilities:

  1. Counter Demo: A stateful Go HTTP server demonstrating state preservation across suspends/resumes, and on-demand actor resumption and routing via the Substrate router.
  2. Sandbox Demo (Antigravity): A secure, sandboxed execution environment (running Alpine Linux) that allows arbitrary shell execution while preserving filesystem state across sessions.
  3. Claude Code Multiplex: Demonstrates oversubscribing physical hardware by multiplexing multiple Claude Code agents onto a limited pool of workers.
  4. Multi-Template: Two ActorTemplates running different binaries share one WorkerPool, even though the templates live in different atespaces.
  5. Request Parking: An oversubscribed pool where the router holds inbound requests until a worker frees up, instead of returning 503.

Documentation & Guides

  • Architecture: How the control plane, node supervisor, and networking stack fit together.
  • API Configuration Guide: Detailed reference for configuring WorkerPools, ActorTemplates, Secrets, and Volumes.
  • Full CLI Documentation: Installation and usage for kubectl-ate.
  • Glossary: Core terms (Actor, Atespace, ActorTemplate, WorkerPool, Worker, ate-api-server, atenet, atelet, ateworker) and how they relate.
  • Integration Repositories: Where integrations live, how their repositories are named, and how fixes flow back to core.
  • Observability Guide: Guide to actor logging, metrics, and distributed tracing.
  • Extending Substrate: How to augment or replace the built-in ingress and egress gateways.
  • Authentication Guide: Which credential people, pods and CI jobs should use with the Substrate API, and how to trust more JWT issuers.
  • Actor JWTs: What an actor JWT contains, how relying parties verify it, and how to rotate the signing key.
  • Federating actor JWTs: Serve the actor JWT issuer publicly and set up a relying party outside the cluster to trust it.
  • Rotating the actor JWT signing key: The rotation steps, how long to wait between them, and replacing a compromised key.
  • Egress Traffic: Which protocols an Actor may reach the outside world with and which are blocked.
  • Enabling man-in-the-middle (MITM) interception for Actor Egress policy: Egress policies such as header injection depend on MITM interception of Actor traffic. This guide explains how an Actor should be configured to enable interception.
  • Request Parking: How the router parks requests through transient worker-pool saturation.
  • Sandbox Asset Cache: How a node caches the sandbox binaries actors run on, decides which runtimes it needs, and evicts to a budget.
  • Upgrade Runbook: Upgrade a running install to a newer supported release, and roll back if needed.
  • Node Storage: How to give snapshot I/O its own disk.
  • Security Guide: Security overview, security principles, and threat modeling.
  • Benchmarking Guide: Locust-based load tests, monitoring stack, and the orchestrated benchmark harness.

Tour

Commands

  • cmd/ateapi: The core control plane API server exposing gRPC endpoints to manage actor and worker lifecycles.
  • cmd/atelet: A node-level DaemonSet that supervises physical worker pods, coordinates snapshotting, and manages state transfers.
  • cmd/atecontroller: A Kubernetes controller that reconciles WorkerPool custom resources.
  • cmd/ate-idp-server: Serves the OpenID discovery document and key set that relying parties use to verify actor JWTs.
  • cmd/atenet: A combined networking controller providing Envoy routing and proxy sidecars.
  • cmd/ateworker-gvisor: An interior-pod helper running inside sandboxed worker pods to execute runsc checkpoint and restore commands.
  • cmd/ateworker-microvm: The microVM peer of ateworker-gvisor, running actors as cloud-hypervisor VMs.
  • cmd/podcertcontroller: A "polyfill" that provides Pod Certificate signers that will eventually ship in upstream Kubernetes (with different names).
  • cmd/kubectl-ate: A CLI tool for managing Agent Substrate resources. See its README.
  • cmd/benchmarking: Synthetic workloads used by the load tests, including glutton, which consumes RAM, disk, and file descriptors on demand.
  • demos/: Sample applications demonstrating Agent Substrate capabilities.

item.title: runkids/skillshare
item.description:
📚 Sync skills, agents, MCP, plugins to all AI CLI tools with one command and simplify team sharing.

https://skillshare.runkids.cc

skillshare

English · Deutsch · Español · Français · 日本語 · 한국어 · Português · Türkçe · 简体中文 · 繁體中文

Your AI coding setup, everywhere.
Manage skills, agents, rules, MCP connections and hooks in one place.
For Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode and more.

Website • Install • Quick Start • Highlights • Screenshots • Desktop App • Docs

Note

Latest: v0.34.0 — Herdr mods are plugins now: the herdr-app target installs, updates and removes Herdr mods and launchers, a mod's panel can open in a copy of your current layout, and the dashboard acts on several plugins at once. skillshare hooks sync NAME1 NAME2 --replace takes over several conflicting native hooks in one go, and two skills with the same name both sync, one under its full path name, instead of both being skipped. The custom theme adds Glass: Everywhere, six more background tints and surface options, and the dashboard can show an Agent's MCP file in the page. Herdr guide → · All releases →

Why skillshare

Switching AI tools should not mean rebuilding your setup. skillshare gives your skills and other AI resources a home you control.

  • Switch tools, keep your skills — edit once, then sync to Claude Code, Codex, Pi and the other tools you use.
  • Take your setup with you — version your source in Git and pull it onto another machine.
  • Share with your team — keep project resources with your code and distribute shared skills through tracked repositories.

One teammate uses Claude Code, another uses Codex. Keep their shared code-review checklist in .skillshare/ alongside the project. New teammates install the declared skills and sync to the configured tools instead of copying instructions from chat. Team onboarding →

Use the desktop app or CLI to manage everything locally, audit skills before use, and choose what each tool receives.

Coming from another tool? Migration Guide · Comparison

CLI and UI Preview

Skill Detail Security Audit
UI Dashboard UI Skills

Installation

Tip

Use skillshare from your desktop. Get Skillshare App for macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows and Linux. First launch helps you install or locate the CLI, choose your AI tools and run your first sync. Installation guide.

Desktop App — visual setup and daily management

Skillshare App puts skills, agents, MCP and hooks in a desktop window. Install the app, open it, and follow first-launch setup.

macOS (Apple Silicon), with Homebrew:

brew tap runkids/tap
brew install --cask skillshare-app

Windows / Linux, or a manual macOS install: Download the latest app installers. See the Desktop App guide for platform details.

CLI: macOS / Linux

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/runkids/skillshare/main/install.sh | sh

The script installs to ~/.local/bin by default, so normal installs and updates do not need sudo. If the installer prints PATH setup instructions, follow them before running skillshare. Add the suggested line to your shell config (such as ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc) for future terminals. Set INSTALL_DIR to use another location.

Windows PowerShell

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/runkids/skillshare/main/install.ps1 | iex

CLI: Homebrew

brew install skillshare

Tip: Run skillshare upgrade to update to the latest version. It auto-detects your install method and handles the rest.

CLI: Nix

nix profile add github:runkids/skillshare

Update with nix profile upgrade skillshare. Requires Nix 2.30+ with flakes enabled; on older Nix or Lix, use nix profile install. NixOS and Home Manager configurations can use the flake's overlays.default.

CLI: PyPI

uv tool install skillshare-cli

Or pipx install skillshare-cli, or pip install skillshare-cli. To try skillshare without installing it, run uvx --from skillshare-cli skillshare. Update with your installer, such as uv tool upgrade skillshare-cli or pipx upgrade skillshare-cli.

GitHub Actions

- uses: runkids/setup-skillshare@v1
  with:
    source: ./skills
- run: skillshare sync

See setup-skillshare for all options (audit, project mode, version pinning).

Shorthand (Optional)

Add an alias to your shell config (~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc):

alias ss='skillshare'

Quick Start

skillshare init            # Create config, source, and detected targets
skillshare sync            # Sync skills to all targets

How It Works

  • macOS / Linux: ~/.config/skillshare/
  • Windows: %AppData%\skillshare\
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Source Directory                         │
│   ~/.config/skillshare/skills/    ← skills (SKILL.md)       │
│   ~/.config/skillshare/agents/    ← agents                  │
│   ~/.config/skillshare/extras/    ← rules, commands, etc.   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ sync
              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
              ▼               ▼               ▼
       ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐
       │  Claude   │   │  OpenCode │   │ OpenClaw  │   ...
       └───────────┘   └───────────┘   └───────────┘
Platform Skills Source Agents Source Extras Source Link Type
macOS/Linux ~/.config/skillshare/skills/ ~/.config/skillshare/agents/ ~/.config/skillshare/extras/ Symlinks
Windows %AppData%\skillshare\skills\ %AppData%\skillshare\agents\ %AppData%\skillshare\extras\ NTFS Junctions for folders (no admin required); file symlinks need Developer Mode, otherwise copied
Imperative (install-per-command) Declarative (skillshare)
Source of truth Skills copied independently Single source → symlinks (or copies)
New machine setup Re-run every install manually git clone config + sync
Security audit None Built-in audit + auto-scan on install/update
Web dashboard None skillshare ui
Runtime dependency Node.js + npm None (single Go binary)

Full comparison →

Highlights

Install & update skills —from GitHub, GitLab, or any Git host

skillshare install github.com/reponame/skills
skillshare update --all
skillshare target claude --mode copy  # if symlinks don't work

Symlink issues? — switch to copy mode per target

skillshare target <name> --mode copy
skillshare sync

Security audit —scan before skills reach your agent

skillshare audit

Project skills —per-repo, committed with your code

item.title: Tencent/LoopForge
item.description:
Self-hosted workflows for coding-agent delivery. Orchestrate CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code with scripts and human approval gates. Includes Local workflows for coding assistants.

https://loopforge.cn

English · 简体中文

Two ways to work · Quick start · LOOPs · Features · Local (Legacy) · FAQ · Docs

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8af401d9-1aae-427c-b4bc-455c12d17beb

80-second product tour (1080p, with sound).

LoopForge is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to Main Bot in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as a LOOP (a reusable delivery workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in.

Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license.

Two ways to work

Chat with Main Bot Run a LOOP
Best for Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off
How it runs Main Bot opens a conversation workspace (a Docker sandbox with your repos) on demand and calls project roles as subagents The engine runs Agent, Script, Human-gate and sub-LOOP nodes in order, in their own sandbox
You stay in control by Queuing or steering messages mid-reply, and pausing, resuming or taking over a running LOOP from chat Approving at human gates, sending work back to a chosen step, retrying or rerunning from any node
Delivers A PR/MR, or a direct merge into a shared branch (mode=direct) Documents, code or a PR, plus per-node artifacts and logs

Both paths track the same requirements, so every change, whether made in chat or by a LOOP, links back to what was asked for and counts toward delivery and cost reports.

The chat home. Type a request, @ a role, skill, requirement, LOOP or repository, and pick the executor, model and permission mode per conversation.

Why LoopForge

Ask a coding agent to "fix this bug" and the result depends on that run. It might skip the plan, forget the tests, review its own code, or stop halfway without anyone noticing. That's fine for a demo, but it isn't how a team ships.

  • Repeatable. Same LOOP, same stages, same checks for every requirement. Start from built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product LOOPs.
  • Separated roles. Planning, implementation, review and testing each get their own prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools. A role works as a LOOP node or as a subagent in chat.
  • Human on the loop. Agents run on their own while you supervise. Pause, steer or take over anytime, and approval gates stop the run where a human must decide: approve, or send the work back to a chosen step.
  • Observable and resumable. Node status, tool traces, logs and artifacts in one place. Pause, retry a failed step, or rerun from any node.
  • Your stack, your servers. Ten coding-agent CLIs as executors, from CodeBuddy, Codex and Claude Code to OpenCode, Cursor CLI and more. GitHub, Skills and MCP as tools. Docker sandboxes or your own machine as the runtime.

Quick start

Install Git and clone the repository first. The installer checks Docker, Compose, Python 3 and curl and offers to install missing components. Python/curl installation supports apt, dnf and yum on Linux; the Compose plugin supports x86_64/arm64 and verifies the official release SHA-256. macOS needs a working Python 3 and Docker Desktop; Homebrew can install missing components. Ordinary Linux users are supported through Docker group access or sudo. Set LOOPFORGE_YES=1 to accept installation prompts. Package and image downloads require internet access.

git clone https://github.com/Tencent/LoopForge.git
cd LoopForge
./start.sh

./start.sh pulls the GHCR release image pinned in compose.yaml without building locally (bash scripts/install.sh does the same). It creates the MySQL and platform services, generates configuration and session secrets, and installs the built-in sandboxes, starter LOOPs and welcome project. Host Go and Node.js installations are not required. Configure model API keys and GitHub authorization after startup. Use ./start.sh logs, stop, restart or pull to manage it, and ./start.sh dev to build the checkout from source.

If downloads from ghcr.io stall, ./start.sh and ./start.sh pull time ghcr.io against the Nanjing University mirror ghcr.nju.edu.cn. Nanjing is used only when its manifest digest matches the digest just read from ghcr.io; the script pulls that digest and tags it back to the name pinned in compose.yaml, which trusts that host because the result is tagged with the official name. A missing official digest, a mismatch, or a failed mirror pull stays on ghcr.io. MIRROR=ghcr.io forces the upstream registry and MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn forces Nanjing; the choice is not written to .env. The GitHub Release records the digest; docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/tencent/loopforge:<pin> should show the same digest after @. compose.yaml stays unchanged. A Docker registry-mirrors entry such as https://docker.nju.edu.cn only accelerates Docker Hub and is not a value for MIRROR.

./start.sh
MIRROR=ghcr.io ./start.sh
MIRROR=ghcr.nju.edu.cn ./start.sh pull

Open the address printed by the installer and create your account; the first one becomes the administrator. The service listens on 0.0.0.0:8090 by default. On a cloud host, the installer reads the public IP from the provider's metadata service and prints it; allow the port in your security group, or put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front. Restrict access to your own IP until the administrator account exists. The home page's quick-access guide walks you through adding a model key, connecting a repository and choosing a LOOP.

For GitLab, Gitea, Gogs and other Git hosts, set up Git SSH to check out and push branches with a personal key. PR/MR and Issue automation requires a hosting API token or a separately configured MCP.

Try it without an API key

New accounts join the LoopForge demo project, which includes a LOOP made only of a script and a human gate:

  1. Switch to the demo project, open Templates, and open Platform check · script & approval.
  2. Click Run LOOP. A real script writes a report, then the run waits for you at the approval step.
  3. Approve it from Needs review or the run page, and watch the run continue to its final artifact.

What you need for real work

I want to… You need
Run the script + approval demo Nothing
Chat with Main Bot, generate a document or a new project An API key for the selected executor
Change an existing repository (in chat or via a LOOP) and open a PR Model credentials and a GitHub repository (connect GitHub in personal settings)
More setup details: executors, GitHub, sandboxes, access model

  • Executors. Choose a CLI and model for chat, requirement clarification, Bot replies, notification reports, run evaluation, or static preview. Each LOOP role can select its own CLI, and built-in templates still default to CodeBuddy. Scheduled prompts use the CLI selected on the schedule. The platform can run without a CodeBuddy installation or key once its workflows use other CLIs. Deployment and upgrade

    Executor Credentials Installation
    CodeBuddy Personal key, or a shared key an administrator configures for chat and LOOP runs Bundled by default, optional on source builds
    Codex Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login In the Docker image
    Claude Code Personal key; a connected execution machine can use its local login Installed from npm on first use, then cached
    OpenCode · Kimi Code · Pi Personal key only Installed from npm on first use, then cached
    DeepSeek Harness Personal key only In the Docker image
    Cursor CLI Personal key only Provider installer on first chat use; not installed into LOOP sandboxes
    Antigravity Personal key, or the connected execution machine owner's existing account login Install the official CLI on the execution machine and in Docker images used for LOOP runs
    ZCode Personal key only Not bundled; install it on the service or execution machine PATH

    The seven agent CLIs after Claude Code keep their model and MCP configuration in a private home directory per run. Antigravity can reuse the execution machine owner's account login in conversation workspaces and native or Docker LOOP sandboxes. Its official CLI refreshes the credential copy, and the Runner saves the refreshed login back to its original local store. Gemini API keys use separate API billing. The other agent CLIs use the responsible user's own key and Base URL from personal settings, including on a connected execution machine. First-use installs need npm or provider access; native deployments need the CLI for the executor you choose.

  • WeCom notifications. The image built from this Dockerfile includes wecom-cli; published images gain it with the next release. Native installations need to install it separately; see Deployment.

  • GitHub is optional. All built-in generic LOOPs run without a repository: product LOOPs deliver documents, and new frontend/backend projects deliver source files in the task workspace. Bug fixes still need source code and reproduction details. Connect a repository when you work on existing code or want PRs.

  • Delivering to a repository. Choose Connect GitHub in personal settings, approve the device code on GitHub and pick your repository (the LoopForge OAuth App is built in; no PAT required, manual PAT entry still works). Set executor credentials (or bind a local execution machine), then either run a project LOOP or ask Main Bot to change the code and submit a PR/MR.

  • Sandboxes. In the default Compose installation, LOOP runs and conversation workspaces both use Docker sandbox containers started through the host Docker socket. Default sandboxes reuse the installed runtime image, so nothing extra is built after installation; custom Dockerfiles still build their own images. Docker socket access grants control of the host daemon, so this setup is for trusted teams, not untrusted multi-tenant isolation. See deployment boundaries. Re-running the installer keeps your data.

  • Accounts and access. New installations listen on all interfaces (existing bind settings are kept) and are designed for a trusted team: signed-in users can read project data across the instance, and teammates can sign up from the login page (AGENTFLOW_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false in .env turns that off). Read the account and access model before exposing it beyond your team.

  • Remote access, HTTPS, separate workers. See Deployment.

  • Hacking on LoopForge itself? bash scripts/dev.sh runs it natively (Go 1.26.11+).

How LOOPs work

A LOOP is the workflow a delivery follows. Agents, scripts and people take part in the same run:

The LOOP designer with a project copy of the built-in bug-fix LOOP. Each step picks a role; failed checks can send the work back to an earlier step.

Node What it does
Agent A role (prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills and MCP tools) that designs, implements, reviews or tests.
Script A deterministic shell step: build, test, lint, generate a report. No AI where AI is not needed.
Human gate Pauses the run until someone checks the artifacts and approves, or sends the work back to a step.
Sub-LOOP Runs another LOOP as a sub-workflow.
Preview build Builds a static site and archives it for review.

Each node declares its artifacts and dependencies, and the engine starts each step once its dependencies complete. Start from a built-in LOOP, adapt its roles, rules and environment to your project, and publish versions as it evolves.

A run waiting at a human gate: approve and continue, add context and rerun the step, or send the work back upstream.

A delivery we actually ran: four CodeBuddy roles planned a Python fix, implemented it, reviewed it independently and summarized the delivery. Three real tests passed; the run waited for human approval, then verified the accepted code had not changed. The reusable acceptance case checks the files and results. See the validation record for scope and known gaps.

Features

Area What you get
Chat workbench Main Bot with per-conversation executor, model and permission mode. @ references for roles, skills, requirements, LOOPs and repositories. Messages queue while a reply runs; Steer interrupts and sends now. Generated files open in a side panel with preview, source and download.
Conversation workspaces On-demand Docker sandboxes with the project's repositories checked out, project roles as native subagents, and direct control of a running LOOP workspace: pause, resume or take over.
LOOP designer Visual canvas with Agent, Script, Human gate, Sub-LOOP and Preview nodes, rework-on-failure edges, validation, version history and publishing. Built-in backend, frontend, bug-fix and product LOOPs.
Roles Reusable definitions: prompt, executor, model, rules, Skills, MCP tools, artifacts and gates, shared across LOOP nodes and chat subagents.
Requirement → delivery Requirements tracked end to end, whether shipped by a LOOP or straight from chat, with PR/MR status tracking, merge detection and direct-branch merges.
Runs & approvals Live node status, tool traces, worker logs, per-node artifact snapshots and workspace previews. A single Needs review inbox for every gate waiting on you.
AI scheduled tasks Recurring agent tasks with full workspace, LOOP and MCP access; a shared market of versioned, parameterized task templates; automatic LOOP dispatch for new requirements.
Insights & cost Engineering metrics, business-domain reports with static HTML/SVG export, and token/cost accounting for LOOPs and conversations at public list prices.
Execution environments Platform workers, Docker sandboxes, or a connected local execution machine using your own tools and repositories.
Team-ready Password accounts, projects and members, light/dark/system themes, an OpenAPI-described HTTP and MCP API. Management pages are in English and Chinese; the chat workbench is Chinese for now.

Built-in LOOPs are read-only blueprints; copy one into your project to run and edit it.

LoopForge Local

Legacy. Previously published versions of LoopForge Local (loopforge-cli) remain available. The Local guide covers installing a fixed version and keeping existing workflows and artifacts.

To use platform projects and LOOPs from a coding assistant, connect CodeBuddy to your LoopForge instance over MCP. Local continues to run its built-in workflows inside the coding assistant without a LoopForge server.

Platform Local (Legacy)
Best for Teams sharing chat workspaces, LOOPs, approvals and history One developer inside an IDE or CLI
Needs Docker + Python 3 Node.js 20+, Python 3.8+ and a coding assistant
Workflows Chat with Main Bot + custom LOOPs on a visual canvas Built-in Classic / Portable workflows
Evidence Shared run details, approvals and metrics in the web workspace Artifacts under artifacts/{task_slug}/ + optional local dashboard

FAQ

Do I need an API key to try it? No. The demo LOOP uses only a script and a human gate. Chat and agent steps need a key for the executor you pick. Model usage is not included; you bring your own credentials.

Do I need GitHub? No. Chat, documents and new projects run in the task workspace. Connect GitHub when you want to change an existing repository or open PRs.

Should I use chat or a LOOP? Use chat to explore and iterate; Main Bot can still open a PR. Once you find a way of working you want every requirement to follow, with fixed reviewers, tests and sign-off, put it in a LOOP. Main Bot can start, pause and take over LOOP runs, so the two paths work together.

How is this different from Dify, n8n or Flowise? Those are general-purpose AI and automation workflow builders. LoopForge is built for software delivery with coding agents: implementer and reviewer roles, Docker sandboxes with real repositories, GitHub delivery, human acceptance gates and run evidence.

How is this different from using Claude Code, Codex, CodeBuddy or another coding CLI directly? LoopForge doesn't replace them; it orchestrates them. Each agent step and each chat turn runs one of those CLIs. LoopForge adds what surrounds it: who does what, in which sandbox, in which order, with which checks, and who signs off.

Is it safe to expose on the internet? New installations listen on all interfaces and target a trusted team. Read the account and access model and set up HTTPS before opening it up. Report vulnerabilities privately via the security policy.

Community

Scan the QR code to join the LoopForge community group.

Contributing

Issues and PRs are welcome: share a use case, report a bug, or improve workflows, integrations and the platform experience. Start with the contributing guide. Security issues go through the security policy.

If LoopForge is useful to you, a star helps others find it.

SDKs, CLI, and MCP Integrate with Python, Java/Kotlin, TypeScript/JavaScript, C#/.NET, or Go SDKs. Use osb from the terminal or connect agents through MCP. SDKs · CLI · MCP
Extensible sandbox protocol Build custom runtime integrations against defined sandbox lifecycle and execution APIs. API specs

Getting Started

Requirements:

  • Docker (required for local execution)
  • Python 3.10+ (required for examples and local runtime)

Install and Configure the Sandbox Server

uvx opensandbox-server init-config ~/.sandbox.toml --example docker

uvx opensandbox-server

# Show help
# uvx opensandbox-server -h

Create a Sandbox and Execute Commands/Scripts

Install the Sandbox SDK

uv pip install opensandbox

Create a sandbox from an alpine image and execute commands and scripts.

import asyncio

from opensandbox import Sandbox
from opensandbox.models import WriteEntry

async def main() -> None:
    # 1. Create a sandbox from the alpine image
    sandbox = await Sandbox.create("alpine")

    try:
        # 2. Execute a shell command
        execution = await sandbox.commands.run("echo 'Hello OpenSandbox!'")
        print(execution.logs.stdout[0].text)

        # 3. Write a script file
        await sandbox.files.write_files([
            WriteEntry(
                path="/tmp/hello.sh",
                data="echo \"Hello $1\"\necho '2 + 2 =' $((2 + 2))",
                mode=755,
            )
        ])

        # 4. Read the file back
        content = await sandbox.files.read_file("/tmp/hello.sh")
        print(f"Content: {content}")

        # 5. Execute the script
        execution = await sandbox.commands.run("sh /tmp/hello.sh OpenSandbox")
        for log in execution.logs.stdout:
            print(log.text)

    finally:
        # 6. Cleanup the sandbox
        await sandbox.destroy()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Examples

Explore examples by what you want your agent to do. Runnable source code lives in examples/.

Use case What you can build Examples
Coding agents Run coding agents in isolated environments to edit files, execute commands, and complete development tasks. Claude Code · Codex CLI · DeerFlow

The OpenSandbox MCP server exposes sandbox creation, command execution, and text file operations to MCP-capable clients such as Claude Code and Cursor.

Read less Logs, JSON, CSV, test output shrink before the model reads them 33.2% fewer input tokens per session (6 synthetic large-tool-output tasks, 18 pairs, Aug 2026 engine)
Auto · new Picks the model and the effort for each ask 0.46× the cost of Opus at xhigh in an interim run (85 tasks); quality gap unresolved
Blocks · new Code mode: agent keeps the scripts it writes and runs them again 397 → 76 tokens for one test run
Waste fixes Finds where your tokens go and fixes it. New: keeps the prompt cache warm while you pause Not measured yet
Browse Web pages come back compressed 14.9% smaller full page than Playwright; 121 vs 15,704 tokens with a query, on one 200-row table

caveman status shows what is on. caveman off browse turns one off. Only Auto needs an account, and it is free. 4.0.0 release notes

Proof

Outside labs first. Ours come with each rock below. Nothing rounded up. Red rows stay red.

Who Setup Result
Adobe Research, CAVEWOMAN paper (cites this repo) Caveman-style output, eight models, five datasets Cost cut 1.4 to 2.4× per model, up to 3×
Elastic, Elasticsearch Labs Caveman mode remade for Elasticsearch, eight live MCP scenarios 63.6% fewer response tokens. "Zero information loss."
JetBrains 86 real coding tasks, paired A/B No measurable quality loss (p = 0.82). 8.5% fewer output tokens

Two findings shaped caveman. Adobe: cavemanning your prompt makes answers worse, so caveman never touches your prompt. JetBrains: agent sessions are mostly code and tool calls, which the voice leaves alone. So caveman grew rocks that shrink what the agent reads and what it runs on.

Say less: the caveman voice

A voice, not broken grammar. Every reply follows the same structure.

Rule What it means
Answer first [thing] [action] [reason]. [next step]. No greeting, no "let me", no recap
One idea per sentence Built on ASD-STE100, the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals: 20 words max, active voice, one term per thing
Meaning never dropped Articles can go. not, never, no, only never go. Numbers and units stay exact
Payload verbatim Code, commands, paths, and error messages untouched, character for character
No theater No "me think". No chatter between tool calls. If caveman phrasing isn't shorter, plain wins
Knows when to stop Security warnings, irreversible actions, and confused users get full sentences. Then grunt resumes
Your prompts stay yours Never rewritten. Research say that backfire

Example run, n=10, not a claim. Ten dev questions on claude-opus-5-5:

Instruction Output tokens
None 6,983
Answer concisely. 4,334
/caveman 4,119
/ultracave 2,693

"Be concise" is the real baseline; new models already know it. On top of it, /caveman cuts 3% more at the median and /ultracave 35% more. Measured on the 3.1.0 rules, not yet re-run. The rules cost about 1,160 tokens of input, and if you pay per request (GitHub Copilot), shorter answers save nothing. Harness · Every case where caveman loses

Only want this rock? The skill alone, no proxy:

npx skills add JuliusBrussee/caveman -g

Type /caveman ($caveman in Codex) if it doesn't start on its own. Say stop caveman to go back.

Other ways in: Claude app and phone, Claude Code plugin, Gemini, every agent at once, Windows, uninstall

Claude on the web, the phone app, or Cowork? No terminal. Add caveman to your Claude account once, in Customize > Plugins: steps. Not tested end to end yet.

# Claude Code plugin, auto-starts every interactive session, subagents too
claude plugin marketplace add JuliusBrussee/caveman && claude plugin install caveman@caveman

# Gemini CLI
gemini extensions install https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman

# Every agent on your machine at once, plus the Claude Code statusline badge (skills need Node.js 18+, the runtime 22.13+)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/v4.2.0/install.sh | bash

Already inside Claude Code? Same rock, slash form. Type these where you talk to Claude:

/plugin marketplace add JuliusBrussee/caveman
/plugin install caveman@caveman

Windows, PowerShell 5.1+:

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/v4.2.0/install.ps1 | iex

On npm 12 or newer, new npm block git install. One-liners above handle it themselves from v3.2.0 on. Old one-liner pinned to v3.1.0 or older still fail there: use one above, or this: npx --allow-git=root -y github:JuliusBrussee/caveman#v4.2.0

Changed your mind: npx -y github:JuliusBrussee/caveman -- --uninstall (on npm 12+, add --allow-git=root too)

Only grabbed the skill? npx skills remove JuliusBrussee/caveman -g take it back out.

Install broke? Open your agent in this repo and say "Read INSTALL.md, install caveman for me." Agent fix own brain.

Read less: 33.2% fewer input tokens

The voice shrinks what the agent says. This shrinks what it reads. Same answers: 18 of 18 right. 6 synthetic large-tool-output tasks, 18 pairs, Aug 2026 engine.

File type The file, through caveman File saved Whole Claude Code session, 3 runs Session saved
CSV 28,041 → 314 98.9% 165,823 → 74,484 55.1%
Logs 22,810 → 348 98.5% 148,807 → 74,068 50.2%
YAML 20,447 → 178 99.1% 132,124 → 71,027 46.2%
Test output 18,806 → 203 98.9% 150,377 → 108,514 27.8%
JSON 18,837 → 281 98.5% 147,975 → 108,939 26.4%
HTML 21,670 → 21,670 none yet 140,687 → 154,641 9.9% worse
All six 130,611 → 22,994 82.4% 885,793 → 591,673 33.2%

The file is each test file through today's compressor alone. The session is the whole agent run, which also carries the system prompt and tools, so it moves less. Honest part: the session run is from August 2026 on an older engine, HTML has no compressor yet so it lost, and each test file hides one record in 61 to 72 KB of noise. Yours will vary. Headroom on the same suite: 15 of 18 right, 6.7% fewer tokens (interval crosses zero; harness not public). Method

Every original stays on your disk. The agent can pull it back any time.

Auto: 0.46x the cost of Opus at xhigh (interim)

New model in your agent's picker. Pick Auto and caveman chooses the model and the effort for each ask. Hard ask, big brain. Easy ask, save rocks.

Setup Tasks solved Cost per try Median time
Opus 5.5, xhigh effort, every ask 44.3% $7.83 35.2 min
Auto, Claude models only 43.7% $3.59 15.9 min
Auto, plus OpenAI and open models 42.9% $3.47 16.7 min

Auto costs 0.46× what Opus 5.5 at xhigh costs. That is 54% saved, in under half the time. 85 real coding tasks from SWE-Interact and SWE-Together, one try each. Honest part: the run is half done, the 0.5-point score gap is too small to tell apart at this size (±7), and most of the saving is Auto lowering effort on easy asks. Already on Opus at medium? Expect less; not measured yet. Full table and limits

caveman login                  # free account. Auto shows up in the model picker
caveman providers add openai   # optional: give Auto more models, on your own key

Works in Claude Code, OpenCode, and Codex on a ChatGPT login, with API keys, Claude Pro/Max, or ChatGPT. Any other model you pick runs as picked. Not signed in: no Auto, nothing sent. What Auto sends

Blocks: code mode, script written once

skills.sh for code mode. Code mode is the agent writing a script instead of making tool call after tool call (Cloudflare, Anthropic). Problem: agent write same script every session, throw it away, write it again. Blocks keep it in your repo, check it every pull request, hand it back.

Input Raw What agents type now Block
go test -v ./..., 326 tests 10,561 397 · | tail -20 76 · test-summary
1.4 MB JSON file 251,893 236 · their own heredoc 227 · json-peek
366-line Go file 3,111 250 · grep -n 489 · grep-defs

Tokens the agent reads back. In one week, agents on one machine wrote the same script 394 times. Purdue measured the habit at up to 9.57% of task cost. grep-defs loses to a bare grep; row stays. Method

Comes with caveman. Eight blocks ready: json-peek · jsonl-stats · test-summary · first-error · wait-for · grep-defs · http-json · replace-in-file. When the agent starts typing a script a block already covers, it gets one line: use the block. Never denies or rewrites a command.

caveman-blocks scan    # what your agents retyped this month. Script text never leaves your machine
caveman-blocks init    # rules and block index into this repo's AGENTS.md

Pre-release (v0.1.0-rc.5). Python only, no sandbox yet. Own repo, own stars: caveman-ai/blocks

Smaller rocks

Rock What it does Measured
caveman learn Ranks where your tokens go, from agent history already on disk. caveman learn implement applies fixes one diff at a time, only on your yes Not yet
Warm cache · new Step away and the provider forgets your session, so the next ask pays full price. Caveman keeps Anthropic's prompt cache warm while you pause, only when your own history says you come back in time. Every warm is listed in caveman stats Not yet
caveman browse <url> A compressed web page for the agent 121 tokens instead of 15,704 for a Playwright snapshot of a 200-row table. Tiny forms lose 2.3×. Bench
/caveman-compress <file> Shrinks memory files like CLAUDE.md, keeps a backup 4,138 tokens instead of 6,198 across five files, 22.8% to 49.1% each, every heading, code block, and path intact. Bench
Middleware Same shrinking inside the Vercel AI SDK, LangChain, OpenAI, or Anthropic call you already make. TypeScript · Python · Every framework · One container for the team Not yet

Commands

In your terminal:

caveman claude                # start an agent on caveman: codex · gemini · opencode · aider · kilo · qwen · hermes · openclaw · pi
caveman status                # what is on, which agents it reaches, one next step
caveman on browse             # switch one rock on or off: output · input · waste-fixes · routing · scripts · browse
caveman login                 # free account, turns on Auto
caveman learn                 # where your tokens go
caveman trial -- claude       # A/B a real session on your own work
caveman shrink -- pnpm test   # compress noisy command output
caveman convert --dry-run     # pixel mode: skills the model reads as images
caveman stats                 # your token history
caveman doctor                # one problem per line, with its fix

In your agent:

Command What it does
/caveman · /ultracave · /megacave The voice, the grunt, the 文言文. /caveman status shows the mode, /caveman off stops it
/caveman-commit One-line Conventional Commit
/caveman-review One finding per line: L42: 🔴 null deref. Guard it.
/caveman-compress <file> Shrinks memory files and backs up the original
/caveman-stats Real token usage for this Claude Code session
/caveman-help Every mode and command on one screen
cavecrew Subagents that find, edit, and review code, then report back in caveman
investigate-first · lean-build · surgical-patch · safe-refactor · migration · verify-and-stop Work patterns that write less code. Your agent picks them up when a task fits
caveman-setup · caveman-discover · caveman-learn · caveman-manage · caveman-optimize · caveman-explore · caveman-evidence-review Drive the proxy from inside your agent

Caveman Cloud

Everything above is for the coding agent you use. Caveman Cloud is for the agents you build.

You ship an agent. Every run costs money. Is it good? Is it cheap? Which change made it worse? Cloud answers.

Cloud does What you get
Observability Every run traced to the work and what it cost. Sets itself up from your repo, your keys, and the logs or OpenTelemetry you already have
Evals Grades how good the answers are, on your own tasks, from your real traffic
Autopilot Proposes a cheaper change, tests it on your recorded work, ships only when the evals say answers are still as good. You approve the pull request
Proof Every number says if it is measured, inferred, or verified. A saving counts only after real traffic shows it

Sign up free  ·  Try the demo  ·  Book a call  ·  Docs

In the wild

ThePrimeagen: "No way this actually works." Watch

Adobe Research: CAVEWOMAN, arXiv, June 2026

JetBrains: "It is fun, and it costs you nothing measurable in quality." Read

Elastic: elastic-caveman on Elasticsearch Labs, April 2026

Hacker News: #1, 904 points

GitHub Trending #1 overall, July 2026 · Trendshift #1 repo of the day, April 2026 · Product Hunt #8 of the day

Started as a joke in April 2026. Now past 100,000 stars. Joke got serious. Voice did not.


Privacy

  • The skill runs on your machine and sends nothing. One exception: /caveman-compress sends the file you compress to your configured model provider.
  • The CLI sends usage stats by default: commands run, token counts, caveman-blocks commands and usage counts, a random install ID, OS, and IP. Never your prompts, code, file paths, or scripts you wrote. One person maintains this for free, and those stats show what to build next. Off for good, Blocks included: caveman telemetry off or DO_NOT_TRACK=1.
  • Auto, only once you sign in and pick it: each ask sends Caveman Cloud your latest ask (with whatever your agent attaches to it, such as CLAUDE.md, memory or @-mentioned files), the one before it, and the end of the agent's last reply, plus each request's tool names, effort, a few agent headers, and the previous request's token counts. On the Free plan Caveman may keep it to improve routing. caveman off routing stops it.
  • Where requests go: from your machine to your provider, or to another provider you added with caveman providers add, on your own key. Only a request routed to a Caveman Cloud model passes through Caveman Cloud, whole (system prompt, tool results, code), on your Caveman project's stored key, billed to that project. caveman providers cloud off stops that.

The full list, and how to delete sent telemetry: SECURITY.md.

item.title: kagent-dev/kagent
item.description:
Cloud Native Agentic AI | Discord: https://bit.ly/kagentdiscord

https://kagent.dev

kagent is a Kubernetes native framework for building AI agents. Kubernetes is the most popular orchestration platform for running workloads, and kagent makes it easy to build, deploy and manage AI agents in Kubernetes. The kagent framework is designed to be easy to understand and use, and to provide a flexible and powerful way to build and manage AI agents.

Getting Started Technical Details Get Involved Reference

Getting Started

  • Your first agent
  • Installation guide

Technical Details

Core Concepts

  • Agents: Agents are the main building block of kagent. An Agent is a Kubernetes custom resource that brings together an agent's behavior and runtime configuration.
  • Agent Templates: A system prompt, a set of tools and subagents, and an LLM configuration define an agent's behavior. You can define this directly in an Agent or share it across agents using an AgentTemplate resource.
  • Harnesses: A Harness defines how an agent runs. Kagent supports its own Go and Python ADKs, Codex, Claude, and custom runtimes, so you can choose the runtime that fits your agent.
  • LLM Providers: Kagent supports multiple LLM providers, including OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Vertex AI, Ollama and custom providers and models accessible via AI gateways. Models are configured through the ModelConfig resource, with provider support depending on the chosen Harness.
  • MCP Tools: Agents can connect to MCP servers that provide tools. Kagent comes with an MCP server with tools for Kubernetes, Istio, Helm, Argo, Prometheus, Grafana, Cilium, and others. Agents connect through RemoteMCPServer resources, which can be shared across agents.
  • Sessions: Sessions keep conversations and task history across interactions. You can suspend and resume an agent, or create a checkpoint and fork a new conversation from it.
  • Observability: Kagent supports OpenTelemetry tracing, which allows you to monitor what's happening with your agents and tools.

Core Principles

  • Kubernetes Native: Manage agent and tool configuration through Kubernetes APIs and familiar kubectl workflows.
  • Extensible: Add custom tools, skills, and runtimes to connect agents to your own systems.
  • Flexible: Choose the models and runtimes that fit your workload, and reuse agent templates across compatible harnesses.
  • Observable: Trace agent, model, and tool execution with OpenTelemetry and your existing observability stack.
  • Declarative: Define agents in YAML, keep configuration in version control, and deploy through GitOps workflows.
  • Testable: Test agents through their public APIs and use task history and traces to diagnose failures.

Architecture

flowchart TD
    UI[UI] --> CONTROLLER[kagent Controller]
    CLI[CLI] --> CONTROLLER
    CONFIG[Kubernetes resources] --> CONTROLLER
    CONTROLLER --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
    CONTROLLER --> SUBSTRATE[Substrate]
    SUBSTRATE --> RUNTIMES[Agent runtimes]
    CONTROLLER -->|A2A| RUNTIMES

Kagent brings together the following components:

  • Controller: The controller watches kagent custom resources, prepares agents to run, and manages their sessions. It exposes gRPC, A2A, and MCP APIs for clients to interact with agents.
  • UI: The UI is a web UI that allows you to manage agents and tools and chat with your agents.
  • Agent Runtimes: Agents run using the Go or Python ADK, Codex, Claude, or a custom runtime, selected by their Harness.
  • Substrate: Substrate runs the agents and manages their lifecycle, including suspension, resumption, and snapshots.
  • PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL stores sessions, tasks, and conversation history so they persist independently of the running agents.
  • CLI: The CLI is a command-line tool that allows you to manage agents and tools and interact with your agents.

For more details on the v1 architecture, including resource definitions and how agents run, see the architecture guide.

Get Involved

We welcome contributions! Contributors are expected to respect the kagent Code of Conduct

There are many ways to get involved:

  • 🐛 Report bugs and issues
  • 💡 Suggest new features
  • 📖 Improve documentation
  • 🔧 Submit pull requests
  • ⭐ Star the repository
  • 💬 Help others in Discord
  • 💬 Join the kagent community meetings
  • 🤝 Share tips in the CNCF #kagent slack channel
  • 🔒 Report security concerns

Roadmap

kagent is currently in active development. You can check out the full roadmap in the project Kanban board here.

Local development

For instructions on running Kagent locally, see DEVELOPMENT.md.

Contributors

Thanks to all contributors who are helping to make kagent better.

item.title: cli/cli
item.description:
GitHub’s official command line tool

https://cli.github.com

GitHub CLI

GitHub CLI, or the gh CLI, is GitHub on the command line. It brings pull requests, issues, and other GitHub concepts to the terminal next to where you are already working with git and your code.

Important

GitHub CLI's PGP signing key rotation for Linux package repositories is effective September 5, 2026; users experiencing package installation or update problems can find solutions in the public announcement.

GitHub CLI is supported for users on GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and supported GitHub Enterprise Server versions, with support for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

Documentation

For installation options see below, for usage instructions see the manual.

Agent skills

An agent skill is available for driving gh from coding agents. Install or update it with the built-in gh skill command:

# Install the skill (user scope recommended)
gh skill install cli/cli gh --scope user

# Update the skill after a `gh` release
gh skill update gh

Contributing

If anything feels off or if you feel that some functionality is missing, please check out the contributing page. There you will find instructions for sharing your feedback, building the tool locally, and submitting pull requests to the project.

If you are a hubber and are interested in shipping new commands for the CLI, check out our doc on internal contributions

Installation

macOS

  • Homebrew
  • Precompiled binaries on releases page

For additional macOS packages and installers, see community-supported docs

Linux & Unix

  • Debian, Raspberry Pi, Ubuntu
  • Amazon Linux, CentOS, Fedora, openSUSE, RHEL, SUSE
  • Precompiled binaries on releases page

For additional Linux & Unix packages and installers, see community-supported docs

Windows

  • WinGet
  • Precompiled binaries on releases page

For additional Windows packages and installers, see community-supported docs

Build from source

See here on how to build GitHub CLI from source.

GitHub Codespaces

To add GitHub CLI to your codespace, add the following to your devcontainer file:

"features": {
  "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/github-cli:1": {}
}

GitHub Actions

GitHub-hosted runners have the GitHub CLI pre-installed, which is updated weekly.

If a specific version is needed, your GitHub Actions workflow will need to install it based on the macOS, Linux & Unix, or Windows instructions above.

For information on all pre-installed tools, see actions/runner-images

Verification of binaries

Starting with v2.93.0, releases of gh are published as immutable releases. For more information, see Immutable releases.

Since version 2.50.0, gh has been producing Build Provenance Attestation, enabling a cryptographically verifiable paper-trail back to the origin GitHub repository, git revision, and build instructions used. The build provenance attestations are signed and rely on Public Good Sigstore for PKI.

There are two common ways to verify a downloaded release, depending on whether gh is already installed or not. If gh is installed, it's trivial to verify a new release:

  • Option 1: Using gh if already installed:

    $ gh at verify -R cli/cli gh_2.62.0_macOS_arm64.zip
Loaded digest sha256:fdb77f31b8a6dd23c3fd858758d692a45f7fc76383e37d475bdcae038df92afc for file://gh_2.62.0_macOS_arm64.zip
Loaded 1 attestation from GitHub API
✓ Verification succeeded!

sha256:fdb77f31b8a6dd23c3fd858758d692a45f7fc76383e37d475bdcae038df92afc was attested by:
REPO     PREDICATE_TYPE                  WORKFLOW
cli/cli  https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1  .github/workflows/deployment.yml@refs/heads/trunk

  • Option 2: Using Sigstore cosign:

    To perform this, download the attestation for the downloaded release and use cosign to verify the authenticity of the downloaded release:

    $ cosign verify-blob-attestation --bundle cli-cli-attestation-3120304.sigstore.json \
      --new-bundle-format \
      --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
      --certificate-identity="https://github.com/cli/cli/.github/workflows/deployment.yml@refs/heads/trunk" \
      gh_2.62.0_macOS_arm64.zip
Verified OK

Comparison with hub

For many years, hub was the unofficial GitHub CLI tool. gh is a new project that helps us explore what an official GitHub CLI tool can look like with a fundamentally different design. While both tools bring GitHub to the terminal, hub behaves as a proxy to git, and gh is a standalone tool. Check out our more detailed explanation to learn more.
